source: Smith, Block & Karney, "Baseline Predictors of Divorce", OSF project hxn84 (https://osf.io/hxn84), data for "Individual, Interpersonal, and Socioeconomic Predictors of Divorce: A 12-Year Prospective Study". Divorce_Data.csv (osf.io/download/srdwb), SHA-256 9fcea8b4...5ed5a08. No licence is stated, so couple rows are not redistributed here: only fitted parameters and aggregates.
target: Probability that a couple still married at the start of a follow-up interval is divorced by its end (couple-level status from both spouses' reports), for nine intervals from baseline (2009-10) to about 12 years later (2021-22). A per-interval probability, not an annual rate; intervals differ in length (see periods).
population: Newlywed (married under about 6 months at baseline), first-married, different-sex couples in Los Angeles County recruited from marriage licences in low-income neighbourhoods, 2009-10; both spouses aged 18+, mostly Hispanic (76%), 11% White, 13% Black. The 368 couples whose status at the last follow-up is known (63 of 431 lost to attrition are excluded). Not representative of U.S. or Los Angeles marriages.
weights: none: the study has no sampling weights; every couple counts once. Results describe these 368 couples, not a population.

training.note: Couple-level dates are not public: intervals are placed at the sample mean years since baseline from the supplement's study timeline. A divorce first reported after a missed wave is placed at the wave that reports it.

how_to_combine: P(still married after interval k) = product over j<=k of (1 - p_j), with p_j the model prediction for interval j (period_XX indicators for the logistic models, period_years for the tree) and every other input as at baseline. Interval ends are about 0.8, 1.6, 2.3, 4.2, 8.8, 9.9, 10.8, 11.4 and 12.0 years after baseline. No follow-up falls between 4.2 and 8.8 years.

inputs.H_Hostility: Husband's report of the past 9 months: 14 items, each 0 never / 1 once or twice / 2 several times / 3 often, about insults or swearing, stomping out, threats to hit, throwing things, pushing/grabbing, slapping/kicking/biting/punching and beating up, BOTH done to them by the spouse and done by them to the spouse. Sum 0-42; sample median 2, 90th percentile 7. Self-report (not observed). If any of this is happening, safety comes first: in the U.S. the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233.
inputs.W_Hostility: Wife's report of the past 9 months: 14 items, each 0 never / 1 once or twice / 2 several times / 3 often, about insults or swearing, stomping out, threats to hit, throwing things, pushing/grabbing, slapping/kicking/biting/punching and beating up, BOTH done to them by the spouse and done by them to the spouse. Sum 0-42; sample median 2, 90th percentile 8. Self-report (not observed). If any of this is happening, safety comes first: in the U.S. the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233.
inputs.H_sat_sum: Husband's relationship satisfaction (self-report). Sum of 8 items (each 1-4 or 1-5): satisfaction with time together, trust, sharing thoughts and feelings, sexual relations, support in difficult times, help with chores, being understood (hopes and dreams), and the marriage overall. Range 8-37; sample median 35, 10th percentile 30.
inputs.W_sat_sum: Wife's relationship satisfaction (self-report). Sum of 8 items (each 1-4 or 1-5): satisfaction with time together, trust, sharing thoughts and feelings, sexual relations, support in difficult times, help with chores, being understood (hopes and dreams), and the marriage overall. Range 8-37; sample median 34, 10th percentile 28.

H_Positivity.description: Husband's positivity (positive mood, warmth/support, affection, humour, endearment, listener responsiveness), coded by trained observers with the Iowa Family Interaction Rating Scales (IFIRS, 1-9 scale), averaged over three videotaped discussions at baseline. Sample range 1.00-5.93, median 2.29.

self_report_proxy.question: When the two of you discuss a disagreement, how often does the husband show warmth, humour, affection or attentive listening?
self_report_proxy.mapping: Each answer maps to the sample's 10th/30th/50th/70th/90th percentile of the observed code.
self_report_proxy.caveat: APPROXIMATION. The model was trained on codes from trained observers watching the couple discuss a problem, not on anyone's self-rating. Self-ratings of conflict behaviour are known to differ from observer codes; this mapping by percentile has not been validated. Treat the result as a rough what-if, not a measurement.

input_blocks.observed_note: Only positivity, negativity and effective communication are observer-coded (IFIRS). Hostility is a self-report questionnaire, even though the paper places it in its couple-behaviour factor.

evaluation: 20 repeats x 5-fold cross-validation by couple (stratified on divorce); penalty chosen by inner 3-fold couple CV on per-period log loss (ridge C grid [0.0003, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3], lasso C grid [0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5], tree depth x min leaf [(1, 60), (2, 60), (2, 120), (3, 120), (3, 240)]); 1000 couple-bootstrap resamples of the repeat-averaged held-out metrics for 95% CIs (evaluation-sample uncertainty, not refitting). AUC at a horizon: divorced by then vs still married then. 6-year horizon not observed.
abstain: couples who are not newlyweds (the models know only the first ~6 months of marriage)
presenting observed-interaction inputs from self-ratings as if they were observer codes (see each input's self_report_proxy.caveat)

population_reference.quantity: predicted probability of divorce by each horizon (1 - product of (1 - per-interval probability)), years since baseline; the couples had married within about 6 months of baseline
population_reference.method: HELD-OUT predictions (20x5-fold couple cross-validation, per-interval probabilities averaged over repeats) of the 'all' model; unweighted quantiles (no sampling weights exist). Subgroup cells need >=50 couples (small_cell marks <100). Aggregates only.
population_reference.small_sample_warning: Only 368 couples (145 divorces). Each subgroup holds 100-250 couples, so the outer percentiles (below p5 and above p95) are set by a handful of couples and are very imprecise; prefer p5-p95. This sample (low-income, mostly Hispanic Los Angeles newlyweds) is not a general population.

Low_income_D.label: Household income below 200% of the 2010 poverty line (1 yes, 0 no)

couple_satisfaction.label: Couple satisfaction third: mean of the two spouses' 8-item sums (H_sat_sum, W_sat_sum)

ood.method: squared Mahalanobis distance on the model inputs; percentile against held-out people (5 person folds)
